words.definition: Describing land that is fit for plowing and raising food crops.
words.example: The valley's arable fields produced wheat and barley every summer.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-rake-able' — ground you can rake, plow, and plant.

words.definition: A fertile soil blend of sand, silt, clay, and decayed organic matter.
words.example: Gardeners prized the dark, crumbly loam for its drainage and richness.
words.mnemonic: LOAM sounds like 'home' — the ideal home for happy plant roots.

words.definition: The dark organic material in soil formed as plants and leaves decompose.
words.example: Years of fallen leaves left the forest floor thick with rich humus.
words.mnemonic: Shares its Latin root with 'humble' and 'human' — all tied to the ground.

words.definition: The crumbly, prepared condition of ground made ready for planting seeds.
words.example: The gardener raked the bed until it reached a fine, workable tilth.
words.mnemonic: TILL + TH: the state of the soil once you finish tilling it.

words.definition: Describing farmland left unseeded for a period to restore its richness.
words.example: They let the north field lie fallow for a year so it could recover.
words.mnemonic: FALL-ow: in fall the field lies bare, resting before it works again.

words.definition: A long, narrow groove cut into the ground by a plow.
words.example: The tractor left neat furrows across the field, waiting for seed.
words.mnemonic: FUR-row: rows carved in the earth's 'fur' where the plow drags.

words.definition: Relating to or characteristic of woods and forest settings.
words.example: They followed a sylvan path shaded by tall oaks and hanging ferns.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'silva' = forest; picture the name Sylvia, a girl of the woods.

words.definition: Living in or relating to trees.
words.example: Sloths are arboreal, spending almost their entire lives up in the branches.
words.mnemonic: ARBOR is Latin for tree — an arbor is a leafy, tree-covered bower.

words.definition: Relating to the peaceful, idealized life of the rural countryside and its shepherds.
words.example: The painting showed a pastoral scene of sheep grazing on rolling green hills.
words.mnemonic: PASTURE + al: picture a shepherd resting in a sunlit pasture.

words.definition: Relating to farming and the practical work of cultivating the land.
words.example: Virgil's georgic verses celebrate plowing, beekeeping, and the labor of the fields.
words.mnemonic: GEORGE comes from Greek 'georgos' = farmer (ge, earth + ergon, work).

words.definition: Relating to farming, cultivated land, or a rural landowning society.
words.example: The reforms redistributed land across the country's largely agrarian economy.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ager' = field — an agrarian society lives by working the fields.

words.definition: The careful management of farming, especially the raising of animals and crops.
words.example: Good animal husbandry kept the herd healthy through the harsh winter.
words.mnemonic: HUSBAND once meant 'master of a household' — the one who tends the farm.

words.definition: The science and practice of growing grapevines, chiefly for wine.
words.example: The region's warm, sloping hillsides make it perfect for viticulture.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'vitis' = vine (as in Vitis vinifera) + culture, meaning cultivation.

words.definition: The art and science of growing garden plants, fruits, vegetables, and flowers.
words.example: She studied horticulture so she could design and plant botanical gardens.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'hortus' = garden (an enclosed yard) + culture, meaning cultivation.

words.definition: The practice of growing and tending forests and trees.
words.example: Sustainable silviculture lets loggers harvest timber without stripping the woodland.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'silva' = forest (see sylvan) + culture — cultivating the forest.

words.definition: A slender, spiraling shoot that a climbing plant uses to grip a support.
words.example: The pea plant sent out a delicate tendril that curled around the trellis.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tender coil' — a tender little coil reaching out for something to hold.

words.definition: A horizontal underground stem that sends out roots and new shoots along its length.
words.example: The gardener divided the iris by cutting its thick underground rhizome into sections.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'rhiza' means root; picture it as a root that has found its 'home' underground.

words.definition: To transfer fertilizing dust between flowers so they can produce seeds or fruit.
words.example: Bees pollinate the orchard each spring, guaranteeing a heavy crop of apples.
words.mnemonic: A bee is a tiny flying taxi — it 'ferries' the yellow dust from bloom to bloom.

words.definition: To join a shoot or bud from one plant onto another so they grow together as one.
words.example: The nurseryman grafted a branch of the rare apple onto sturdy, disease-resistant rootstock.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'craft' — you craft two separate plants into a single living one.

words.definition: To cut away dead or overgrown branches to shape a plant or improve its health.
words.example: Each winter she pruned the roses hard so they would bloom fully by June.
words.mnemonic: A shrivelled 'prune' is a plum with the excess removed — you strip a plant down the same way.

words.definition: Fresh, lush green vegetation, or the vivid greenness of such growth.
words.example: After a week of rain the barren slope was suddenly clothed in bright verdure.
words.mnemonic: 'Verde' is Spanish and Italian for green — verdure is greenness made into a noun.

words.definition: The large, often feathery leaf of a fern or palm.
words.example: A single fern frond uncurled slowly in the damp morning light.
words.mnemonic: 'Frond' looks like 'fern' with a flourish — picture the fern's fanning feather.

words.definition: The main woody trunk of a tree.
words.example: He pressed his palm against the rough, mossy bole of the ancient oak.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'bowl' — imagine a huge round column of wood you could hollow into a bowl.

words.definition: A small cluster of trees or shrubs.
words.example: The startled deer vanished into a copse at the edge of the meadow.
words.mnemonic: Say it like 'cops' — a small squad of trees huddled together for a stakeout.

words.definition: An area of small trees regularly cut back near the base to encourage fresh growth.
words.example: The old hazel coppice was harvested every seven years for firewood and fencing.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'copy' — cut it low and the stump 'copies' itself with a burst of new shoots.

words.definition: A dense growth of shrubs, bushes, or small trees.
words.example: The rabbit darted into a thorny thicket where the fox could not follow.
words.mnemonic: 'Thick' + '-et' — a thick-set tangle of bushes packed too close to walk through.

words.definition: A small, secluded, usually wooded valley.
words.example: They spread their picnic in a shady dell hidden between two rolling hills.
words.mnemonic: The nursery rhyme 'the farmer in the dell' — he lives down in a snug little hollow.

words.definition: An open, grassy clearing within a forest.
words.example: Sunlight poured into the glade where the crowded trees finally thinned out.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside 'glade' is 'glad' — the sun is glad to reach the one open space in the woods.

words.definition: Open, uncultivated land covered with low shrubs and rough grasses.
words.example: The windswept heath stretched for miles, purple with tough flowering shrubs.
words.mnemonic: Picture Heathcliff striding the wild open moors — that bleak shrubby ground is his namesake.

words.definition: Low, flat, waterlogged land that is often marshy and rich in minerals.
words.example: Wading birds nested among the reeds of the misty fen at dawn.
words.mnemonic: Short and soggy like the sound itself — think of England's foggy 'Fens', flat and forever wet.

words.definition: Soft, waterlogged ground made of decaying plant matter, too spongy to walk on easily.
words.example: Her boots sank ankle-deep as she crossed the bog, each step making a wet sucking sound.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'log' — picture a log slowly sinking into soggy peat.

words.definition: An expanse of deep, sticky mud that traps whatever tries to move through it.
words.example: The truck's wheels spun uselessly, sunk to the axles in the mire after the storm.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'tire' — imagine a tire stuck fast and spinning in the muck.

words.definition: The wide tidal zone where a river's fresh water blends with salty ocean water.
words.example: Salmon paused in the estuary, adjusting to the salt before continuing upstream to spawn.
words.mnemonic: From Latin aestus, 'tide' — the tide's meeting place where river greets sea.

words.definition: Describing soil or sediment carried and dropped by moving rivers or floods.
words.example: The alluvial plain was famously fertile, enriched each year when the river overflowed.
words.mnemonic: Latin alluere, 'to wash against' — water washes the loose soil into place.

words.definition: Fine particles of earth carried by water and settling as a smooth sediment.
words.example: Over decades, silt filled the reservoir until it held barely half its original water.
words.mnemonic: Tiny grit that settles 'silently' at the bottom — silt is quiet and fine.

words.definition: Relating to the region along a coast or the edge of the sea.
words.example: Crabs and clams thrive in the littoral zone, exposed at low tide and drowned at high.
words.mnemonic: From Latin litus, 'shore' — think 'litter-al,' the strip where waves litter shells.

words.definition: Relating to the banks and immediate edges of a river or stream.
words.example: Planting willows along the riparian strip kept the streambank from washing away.
words.mnemonic: Latin ripa means 'bank' — riparian runs right along the river's rim.

words.definition: Relating to or found in lakes.
words.example: The lacustrine sediments revealed thousands of years of the lake's quiet history.
words.mnemonic: Latin lacus, 'lake' — a lacustrine creature lounges in the lake.

words.definition: Relating to the cool, forested slopes and zones of high uplands.
words.example: Above the foothills, the montane forest gave way to firs and increasingly thin air.
words.mnemonic: 'Mont' (as in mountain) + terrain — the terrain of the mountainside.

words.definition: Relating to the cold northern regions and their evergreen forests.
words.example: Wolves and moose roam the boreal wilderness that rings the Arctic Circle.
words.mnemonic: Boreas was the Greek god of the north wind — boreal is his frozen domain.

words.definition: A vast, flat, treeless grassland found in dry temperate regions.
words.example: Horsemen galloped for days across the Mongolian steppe without passing a single tree.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'step' — you step endlessly over flat grass and never arrive.

words.definition: Describing trees or shrubs that drop their leaves each autumn.
words.example: In October the deciduous oaks blazed orange, then stood bare by late November.
words.mnemonic: Latin decidere, 'to fall off' — the tree makes a 'decision' to let leaves fall.

words.definition: Describing cone-bearing evergreen trees with needle-like foliage.
words.example: The coniferous slopes stayed dark green all winter while the valley oaks went bare.
words.mnemonic: 'Cone' + Latin ferre, 'to bear' — it bears cones.

words.definition: Describing plants with soft, green stems rather than hard woody ones.
words.example: She filled the border with herbaceous perennials that died back to the soil each winter.
words.mnemonic: 'Herb' + '-aceous' — full of herb-like, tender, non-woody softness.

words.definition: Describing a plant with thick, fleshy parts that store water for dry spells.
words.example: The succulent survived weeks of neglect, its fat leaves hoarding every drop of moisture.
words.mnemonic: From Latin sucus, 'juice' — you could almost 'suck' juice from its plump leaves.

words.definition: To be present in very large amounts or numbers.
words.example: In spring the meadow abounds with wildflowers and buzzing bees.
words.mnemonic: a-BOUND — picture things bouncing around in huge, plentiful bounds.

words.definition: A plant variety produced and named through intentional selective breeding by growers.
words.example: This apple cultivar was bred for sweetness and resistance to frost.
words.mnemonic: CULTIVAR = CULTIVAted + VARiety — a plant humans deliberately bred.

words.definition: A young plant shoot cut for grafting, or a descendant of a notable family.
words.example: The gardener grafted a pear scion onto sturdy quince rootstock.
words.mnemonic: SCION sounds like 'sigh-on' — the young twig you set on a rootstock.

words.definition: To cut a tree's upper branches back to the trunk, encouraging bushy regrowth.
words.example: Each winter the council workers pollard the willows lining the canal.
words.mnemonic: POLL once meant 'head' — you lop off the tree's head.

words.definition: The craft of trimming shrubs and trees into ornamental, sculpted shapes.
words.example: The palace garden featured topiary peacocks clipped from dense boxwood.
words.mnemonic: TOP-iary — you shape the TOP of a bush into living art.

words.definition: A shady garden shelter formed by trees or climbing plants overhead.
words.example: They rested beneath the rose arbor, shaded from the afternoon sun.
words.mnemonic: ARBOR holds the Latin 'arbor-' for tree — a leafy tree-shelter.

words.definition: A pleasant, leafy shady spot or shelter beneath trees in a garden.
words.example: The lovers slipped away to a secluded bower behind the hedges.
words.mnemonic: BOWER sounds like 'bough-er' — made of leafy boughs above you.

words.definition: An outdoor framework of posts and crossbeams supporting climbing plants overhead.
words.example: Wisteria draped across the pergola, dappling the patio with purple shade.
words.mnemonic: A PERGOLA is a 'per-GO-la' arch you go under, dripping with vines.

words.definition: A lattice framework of crossed strips supporting climbing plants against a wall.
words.example: She trained the sweet peas up a white trellis beside the door.
words.mnemonic: TRELLIS = 'trail-lattice' — vines trail up the crisscrossed slats.

words.definition: Grassy land where livestock roam and feed on growing plants.
words.example: The dairy cows spent the summer on the hillside pasture.
words.mnemonic: PASTURE — cows 'pass' the hours eating grass there.

words.definition: To wander about searching for food or supplies, especially in the wild.
words.example: The deer forage at dusk, nosing through the underbrush for shoots.
words.mnemonic: FORAGE sounds like 'for-a-graze' — roaming for something to eat.

words.definition: Dried hay or feed given to cattle, horses, and other farm animals.
words.example: They stacked bales of fodder in the barn to last through winter.
words.mnemonic: FODDER sounds like 'food-er' — food for the herd.

words.definition: Green crops packed and fermented in storage to feed animals in winter.
words.example: The farmer packed chopped maize into the pit as silage for the herd.
words.mnemonic: SILAGE lives in a SILo — the '-age' that fills the silo.

words.definition: Dry feed for livestock, or food and provisions in general.
words.example: The stable boy measured out the horses' provender before dawn.
words.mnemonic: PROVENDER ≈ 'PROVIDE dinner' — what you provide for the animals.

words.definition: To separate grain from its husks using a current of air.
words.example: The farmers tossed the threshed wheat skyward to winnow the chaff.
words.mnemonic: WINNOW — the WIND blows the light husks away.

words.definition: To beat harvested cereal plants so the edible grain comes loose from the straw and husks.
words.example: After the wheat was cut, the laborers would thresh it with heavy flails until the kernels fell free.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'thrash' — you thrash the stalks to knock the grain loose.

words.definition: A heavy farming frame fitted with spikes or discs, dragged to break up and level plowed soil.
words.example: The tractor pulled the harrow across the field, crumbling the clods the plow had left behind.
words.mnemonic: HARROW has teeth like a row of ARROWs raking through the earth.

words.definition: A swollen underground stem that stores food for a plant, such as a potato.
words.example: She dug into the soil and pulled up a fat tuber, brushing off what would become next spring's seed potato.
words.mnemonic: Say 'TUBE-er' — a fat tube of starch swelling underground.

words.definition: A short, rounded underground stem base in which certain plants store food, as in crocuses.
words.example: When she lifted the gladiolus, a firm corm clung to the roots, ready to be replanted next season.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'core' — a solid little core of food stored below the ground.

words.definition: The ring of leaf-like parts forming the outer protective layer of a flower bud.
words.example: Before the rose opened, a green calyx cupped the petals, peeling back as the bloom unfurled.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'chalice' — a cup that holds the flower before it opens.

words.definition: One of the small leaf-like segments that encloses and guards a developing flower bud.
words.example: Each green sepal folded back one by one, revealing the bright petals of the tulip beneath.
words.mnemonic: SEPAL = it SEParates and shields the petal; it even rhymes with 'petal'.

words.definition: The pollen-producing male part of a flower, a slender stalk topped by an anther.
words.example: A bee brushed against the stamen and flew off dusted with yellow pollen.
words.mnemonic: STAMEN ends in 'men' — it's the male reproductive organ of the flower.

words.definition: A rough, thorny shrub that grows in tangled thickets, especially the wild blackberry.
words.example: Reaching for the ripe blackberries, she snagged her sleeve on a bramble and pulled back a scratched hand.
words.mnemonic: Blend of 'scramble' and 'ramble' — thorny vines that ramble and scramble everywhere.

words.definition: A prickly wild shrub with thorny stems, such as a wild rose or blackberry.
words.example: The path narrowed until a tangle of briar blocked the way, its thorns catching their coats.
words.mnemonic: Think of Br'er Rabbit's thorny patch — one prick and you cry 'aye-er!'

words.definition: A tall, coarse fern that spreads across open hillsides and woodland clearings.
words.example: They waded through waist-high bracken, its feathery fronds brushing their arms as they climbed the moor.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'bracket' — ferns that bracket the whole hillside in green.

words.definition: A spiny evergreen shrub with bright yellow flowers, common on heaths and moorland.
words.example: The hillside blazed yellow with gorse, though its spines kept the grazing sheep well away.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'coarse' — gorgeous yellow blooms on a coarse, prickly bush.

words.definition: A thorny evergreen heath shrub bearing fragrant yellow blossoms, found on poor, sandy ground.
words.example: Bees hummed over the furze, drawn to its coconut-scented blooms despite the sharp spines.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'furs', yet it's all prickles — a surprise that stings the hand expecting softness.

words.definition: A grass-like plant with triangular stems that grows in marshes and along wet ground.
words.example: Along the pond's edge, clumps of sedge rustled, their sharp stems swaying over the muddy bank.
words.mnemonic: It grows on the 'edge' of the water, and 'sedge' rhymes with edge.

words.definition: A crusty or leafy organism of fungus and alga living together, growing on rocks and bark.
words.example: Grey-green lichen crusted the old gravestone, slowly spreading across the weathered granite.
words.mnemonic: Pronounced 'LY-ken' — picture it 'likin'' to cling onto bare rock.

words.definition: A tiny reproductive cell from which a fungus, fern, or moss can grow without seeds.
words.example: A single spore, carried on the wind, was enough to start a new colony of mould on the damp wall.
words.mnemonic: 'Spore' sounds like 'spread more' — one drifts off and more growth appears.

words.definition: The threadlike underground network through which fungi absorb nutrients and grow.
words.example: When she lifted the rotting log, a web of pale mycelium laced the damp soil beneath it.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'MY-CELL-ium' — picture 'my cells' branching into countless threads through the earth.

words.definition: The uppermost layer of leaves and branches spreading over a forest.
words.example: Sunlight barely reached the trail, filtered to a green dusk by the dense canopy far overhead.
words.mnemonic: A 'canopy' bed has a cover stretched above you — the forest's canopy is the leafy cover above the trees.

words.definition: An area of ground covered with a smooth, even growth of short grass.
words.example: The children raced across the springy sward and collapsed, laughing, near the pond.
words.mnemonic: 'Sward' sounds like 'sword' — imagine a sword laid flat, glinting on a neat green lawn.

words.definition: Green, leafy plants growing in a field, especially those eaten by grazing animals.
words.example: The cattle wandered the meadow all morning, cropping the tender herbage down to stubble.
words.mnemonic: 'HERB' + 'age' — a whole age's worth of soft green herbs blanketing the ground.

words.definition: Grassy land on which livestock graze, or the grazing that such land provides.
words.example: The shepherd drove his flock uphill to find fresher pasturage in the summer valley.
words.mnemonic: 'Pass-your-age' — picture cows peacefully passing their whole age chewing over grassy ground.

words.definition: To spend time in dull inactivity, doing little and making no real progress.
words.example: After exams he did nothing but vegetate on the couch for a week, remote in hand.
words.mnemonic: Act like a 'vegetable' — sit rooted and motionless, doing absolutely nothing.

words.definition: To divide or spread out into many branches or smaller subdivisions.
words.example: As the investigation ramified, fresh leads sprouted in three different cities at once.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ramus' = branch; picture a RAM whose antlers ramify into ever-splitting prongs.

words.definition: The cluster or arrangement of blossoms on a single stalk of a plant.
words.example: The botanist sketched the wisteria's drooping inflorescence, dozens of blooms cascading from one stem.
words.mnemonic: 'IN-FLOR-escence' — think 'in flora,' a whole grouping of blooms gathered on one stem.

words.definition: To strip a plant or tree of its leaves, often through chemicals or disease.
words.example: The invasive beetles can defoliate an entire oak within a single dry summer.
words.mnemonic: 'DE-' (remove) + 'FOLI' (leaf) — literally to de-leaf, tearing every leaf away.

words.definition: A tiny blossom, especially one of many that together make up a larger cluster.
words.example: She snapped the broccoli into bite-sized florets and tossed them onto the roasting pan.
words.mnemonic: 'FLOR' (flower) + '-et' (little) — a little flora, a mini bloom you could hold on a fingertip.

words.definition: A garden or park where many kinds of trees are grown for study and display.
words.example: They spent Sunday wandering the arboretum, comparing maples gathered from across the world.
words.mnemonic: 'ARBOR' (tree) + '-etum' (place of) — a place devoted entirely to trees, an arbor museum.

words.definition: To take great pleasure in something comfortable, relaxing fully and without any hurry.
words.example: She luxuriated in the steaming bath, letting the whole day's tension slowly dissolve.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'luxury' inside it — to bask in pure luxury, savoring every indulgent moment.

description: advanced and low-frequency — nature and cultivation
